Biała Podlaska Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Biała Podlaska, Poland

Demolished. Biała Podlaska's Jewish community may date to 1575, according to a hypothesis by the historian M. Hendl, though the source itself notes there is no confirming evidence; the earliest solid record comes from 1621, when the town's owner, Prince Aleksander Ludwik Radziwiłł, issued a regulation limiting Jewish households to 30, by which point an organized kehilla — subordinate to the larger community in Brest-Litovsk — already existed. The community grew to a majority of the town, 65 percent by 1931, and mid-19th-century Biała Podlaska hosted rabbis from several Hasidic dynasties; several thousand Jews were shot in the town in mid-1942, with the rest deported to Sobibór, Treblinka, and Majdanek. This cemetery, likely established in the first quarter of the 17th century and documented on a 1777 city plan, was used until the early 19th century, when a newer cemetery took over; its original brick fence was demolished by German forces during WWI — an unusually early instance of wartime destruction in this collection — and the site was further devastated in WWII. A cinema, still standing today, was built on part of the grounds after 1960, and in 1995 a monument to Poles deported to Siberia was erected on the site; no tombstones predating the early 19th century have ever been found.
